summary: Describes Zstandard (zstd), a lossless data compression mechanism, and registers a media type, a content encoding and a structured syntax suffix for carrying zstd data in MIME. Despite the name, the document is informational and the format is not an IETF standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Zstandard, or zstd, compresses data so a decoder can restore the original bytes exactly. Its frames describe how to read blocks of compressed or uncompressed data. This RFC defines the format and registers names for using zstd data in media types and HTTP.

questions: what is the zstd magic number
subtitle: The Zstandard frame format and the names used to label compressed data.

tldr.problem: Programs need a precise format for losslessly compressed data and shared labels for carrying that data in media types and HTTP content.
tldr.mechanism: Zstandard stores data in frames made of blocks. Compressed blocks use Huffman-coded literals and sequences that copy data from earlier output; the RFC also registers application/zstd, the zstd content coding, and the +zstd suffix.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8878 is Informational, not an Internet Standards Track specification. It obsoletes RFC 8478 and has been updated by RFC 9659.

sections.title: What Zstandard Defines
sections.content:
Zstandard, also called zstd, is a lossless compression format: successful decompression reproduces the original bytes. The format is designed for files and streams and does not provide random access to compressed data.

The RFC registers a media type, an HTTP content coding, and a structured syntax suffix for zstd-compressed content. Despite the name, the document is published for informational purposes and is not an Internet Standards Track specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Zstd compresses data without changing the original content. This RFC also gives software standard names for identifying zstd-compressed data.

sections.title: Frames, Headers, and Blocks
sections.content:
A zstd stream contains one or more independent frames. A frame starts with the four-byte magic number 0xFD2FB528, followed by a header and one or more data blocks; an optional four-byte checksum can follow the blocks. Concatenated frames decompress to concatenated data.

The frame header provides information such as the required window size, an optional dictionary identifier, and an optional uncompressed content size. Each block has a three-byte header identifying its type and size. Blocks can be raw, run-length encoded, or compressed; the reserved block type must be rejected as corrupt data.
sections.plainLanguage: A frame tells a decoder how to interpret its blocks and how much memory it may need. Each block says whether its content is raw, repeated, or compressed.

sections.title: How Compressed Blocks Rebuild Data
sections.content:
A compressed block contains literals and sequences. Literals are bytes to copy directly; each sequence says how many literals to copy and then how much earlier data to copy from a stated offset.

Huffman coding encodes literals. Finite State Entropy (FSE) encodes the sequence symbols and Huffman headers. These bitstreams are read backward from their end. The format also remembers three recent offsets so later sequences can refer to them compactly.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of storing repeated data again, a sequence can tell the decoder to copy bytes it has already produced. Huffman coding and FSE encode the instructions and literal bytes.

sections.title: Dictionaries and Memory Limits
sections.content:
A dictionary is data that both sides already have. The compressor can refer to that data as if it appeared before the current input, which can help compress smaller inputs. Dictionaries are supplied separately; the frame can carry a dictionary identifier, but this RFC does not specify how a decoder obtains the dictionary.

A decoder needs enough memory for the frame's window and may reject frames that exceed its authorized limit. The RFC recommends support for window sizes up to 8 MB. Content using the registered media type should not use a dictionary under this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A dictionary is shared data that compressed content can refer to without including it in the frame. A decoder can reject a frame if its memory needs exceed local limits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Do not compress secret content together with content generated by a third party. An attacker may use changes in compressed size to infer parts of the secret; the RFC cites the CRIME attack as an example.

Decoders must check frame sizes and memory requirements to prevent malformed data from causing out-of-bounds reads or writes. The RFC recommends fuzz testing. It also notes that skippable frames can carry tracking information and that dictionaries from third parties can create resource-exhaustion risks.
sections.plainLanguage: Compression can reveal information about a secret if it is combined with attacker-controlled content. Decoders must also check size and memory requests before processing a frame.

fields.name: Last_Block
fields.desc: Marks the final block in the frame.

fields.name: Block_Size
fields.desc: Content size, or the repeat count for an RLE block.
